entries.title: Shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?
entries.summary: The US is reportedly considering ways to convert "dark tankers" into legitimate vessels, allowing them to transport crude oil that is not subject to sanctions.
entries.content:
Europe

Russia shadow fleet sanctions: Can the EU act if the US pulls back?

October 29, 2026

The US is reportedly considering ways to convert "dark tankers" into legitimate vessels, allowing them to transport crude oil that is not subject to sanctions.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has increasingly relied on a so-called shadow fleet to bypass Western sanctions and transport its oil around the world.

Other heavily sanctioned countries, including Iran and Venezuela, have also been accused of using such vessels to export petroleum products.

These tankers often rely on deceptive practices like turning off their location transponders to evade detection and conceal the cargo's true origins or destinations.

The fleet, which consists largely of aging, uninsured and poorly maintained tankers, has raised widespread concern across the shipping industry. Yet it has expanded rapidly in recent years and now accounts for nearly 19% of global oil tanker capacity, according to estimates by financial intelligence firm S&P Global.

"The shadow fleet is a scourge," Elisabeth Braw, senior fellow at the think tank Atlantic Council, said, adding that "it is in nobody's interest" to have these ships sailing around in the world's oceans.

She pointed out that these tankers undermine the maritime order and increase the risk of accidents and environmental damage.

"Every country should use its leverage with Russia to ask it not to use the fleet," she told DW, noting that ultimately all countries suffer the consequences.

Easing sanctions to reduce freight rates?

To clamp down on the fleet and curb Russia's oil export revenues, the United States and European countries have stepped up efforts to intercept tankers accused of violating sanctions.

The Trump administration, however, is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels and allowing them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.

A US official told Reuters earlier this month that the move was intended to ease record-high global freight rates.

Lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet "would decrease the effectiveness of the sanctions regime overall," said Michael Carpenter, senior fellow for Transatlantic Affairs at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Such a move "rewards the aggressor and helps Moscow gain revenues to continue attacking Ukraine," he told DW.

"This is the exact opposite of what the US should be doing if it wants to end the war."

Carpenter, who previously served as US ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said any sanctions relief would also put the US and the EU "strategically at odds with each other, with the EU clearly backing Ukraine and the US increasingly supporting Russia's financial goals."

This view is shared by Ben Harris, vice president and director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution.

Lifting sanctions on shadow fleet tankers would "make it substantially easier for Russia to trade its oil at market rates," he said, pointing out that it would "improve its government finances since so much revenue is tied to energy markets."

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, however, rejected suggestions that the US was removing sanctions from shadow fleet tankers.

"We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers," Bloomberg quoted Wright as saying last week. "There is no removing of sanctions," he stressed, adding that the US government was working with investors who buy idle sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.

"We're going to move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet,'" Wright said. "They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore."

The US government has yet to unveil a detailed plan for shadow fleet tankers.

Trump's deal with Putin raises concerns

The proposal follows a deal that US President Donald Trump struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin this month to allow sales of Russian diesel onto global markets.

The agreement was seen as part of Trump's efforts to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.

The US president also waived broad new sanctions on Russia authorized by ​a recent legislation, which targeted Moscow's energy revenues and threatened tariffs against the world's largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.

The decision was sharply criticized by Ukraine and its European allies over concerns that it could undermine the credibility of sanctions and weaken Western economic pressure on Moscow.

Harris said that "the US sanctions carry outsized weight because of the threat [for countries and businesses] of being cut off from the US financial system."

What can the EU do?

If the US steps away from its sanctions on the shadow fleet, he argued, "the responsibility shifts to European policymakers." Still, they have "less effective options because of the diminished threat of severing financial ties."

Still, the expert stressed that Europe has some tools, pointing to the continent's key role in global shipping and insurance services.

"They can implement measures demanding that tankers carry legitimate and established insurance when traveling through their waters," he said, noting that it "would mean that many shadow fleet tankers could not in practice legally transport Russian oil."

Harris added that European policymakers could also pressure countries worldwide to better regulate the tankers flying their flags.

Carpenter said even if US eases some restrictions, the EU will have no choice but to continue enforcing its sanctions on these vessels.

"The vast majority of the shadow fleet traverses the Baltic Sea and exits it via the Danish Strait," he noted, adding that the EU is "uniquely positioned to board and inspect vessels moving through this key chokepoint."

But Russia has threatened to seize ships belonging to European countries in retaliation for interdicting and seizing Russian vessels suspected of being part of the shadow fleet.

And without US backing, Carpenter said, "it will be harder for EU countries to take on the burdens and risks of sanctions enforcement."

Braw echoed this view, saying that Ukraine's European allies will have to remain united and continue working closely with partners such as Japan, Australia and Canada. Nevertheless, she stressed that what they can achieve on their own "is far less than what they can achieve if the US is part of the team."

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: Ukraine: 13 killed in Russian drone strike on crowded Dnipro train station
entries.summary: A jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform at a civilian station in Dnipro, killing and injuring passengers who were waiting to board a train. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific."
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: 13 killed in Russian drone strike on train station

October 29, 2026

A jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform at a civilian station in Dnipro, killing and injuring passengers who were waiting to board a train. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific."

At least 13 people were killed and five more injured when a Russian drone struck a passenger train which was stopped at a station in the eastern Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday morning.

According to Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, a jet-powered drone struck a platform on which people were waiting to board a regional train to Zaporizhzhia, about a two-hour journey to the south.

"Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said.

Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three drones in the daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.

In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them.

Dnipro city mayor Borys Filatov also confirmed the incident, which he called a "tragedy."

Zelenskyy issues veiled Trump criticism after 'horrific' attack

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific" and demanded international action from Kyiv's allies.

"Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he said.

"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating?" he asked, referring to a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin which saw some sanctions on Russia eased and the release of Russian diesel stocks onto global markets.

French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his "deep concern" that Russia continues to "opt for escalation" by targeting civilians.

"In this context, we must aim for much more than a localized ceasefire — such as the one recently negotiated for Oleshky," the French president said on social media, describing Moscow’s rejection of "all proposals to that end" as "intolerable."

"Together, we must redouble our efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace and bring Russia to the negotiating table," he said.

How Russia targets Ukrainian trains

Russia has been targeting Ukrainian trains and stations since day one of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing railway workers and passengers.

Faced with an increasing number of Russian drone attacks, Ukrainian trains began large-scale passenger evacuations this year — often while trains are already mid-journey.

In September alone, more than 5,800 trains had to be evacuated due to the threat of strikes, Ukrzaliznytsia told the AFP news agency.

Most evacuations take place in regions near the front line, in the south and east of the country: in Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia.

When a potential Russian strike is detected, the train comes to a halt and passengers are required to leave their carriages and wait at a safe distance until the danger has passed.

With commercial air travel in Ukraine shut down due to the war, the country's vast railway network has become essential for transporting people and goods, as well as for entering and leaving Ukraine.

Ukraine: More Russian attacks

Also on Thursday, authorities reported at least five other fatalities resulting from other Russian attacks across Ukraine.

A strike on the city center of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, according to the head of the city's military administration.

Elsewhere, a drone slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several — including a six-year-old.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: European Central Bank (ECB) head Christine Lagarde to step down in February, before her term ends
entries.summary: European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde is to resign nine months ahead of the end of her 8-year term. European Council President Antonio Costa has said the process to find a successor is underway.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde is to resign nine months ahead of the end of her 8-year term. European Council President Antonio Costa has said the process to find a successor is underway.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the European Central Bank for seven years, has announced that she is stepping down prematurely from the position.

"European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a statement.

European Council President Antonio Costa said a process to find her successor would start immediately.

The announcement comes ahead of a key meeting of the bank this week that is likely to focus on France's deteriorating public finances.

No reason has so far been given for Lagarde's premature departure, but there has been speculation that she would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose her successor before French elections in the spring that could see a eurosceptic far-right victory influence the choice.

Her term, which began on November 1, 2019, would normally have ended at the end of October 2027.

Lagarde, a former French finance minister, was also head of the International Monetary Fund from 2011 to 2019.

Lagarde 'provided steady and determine stewardship' — Costa

Costa praised Lagarde's leadership during her seven-year stint at the ECB helm, a period in which the EU and the world faced great challenges.

"Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa posted on social media.

"To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision," Costa said.

Lagarde herself has voiced satisfaction with her record.

"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde, a French economist, said in a short video shared on ​social media.

The ECB head is chosen by the leaders of the 21 eurozone countries.

ECB to decide interest rate, discuss France

The announcement of Lagarde's imminent departure comes as the ECB is to hold a meeting this week where it is expected to keep its ​deposit rate at 2.5%, while signaling that this is likely to rise again before the end of the year.

The bank has already raised interest rates twice since June in a bid to curb inflation fueled by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.

However, Thursday's meeting is also likely to focus on the fiscal and political crisis in France, Europe's second-biggest economy.

French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, rose to their highest level in 25 years last week amid a deadlock over next year's budget.

Recent protests, at which many demonstrators were calling for more spending on public services, were also marred by considerable violence.

There has been speculation as to whether the ECB could, for the first time, use the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI),  a crisis-fighting tool that allows the bank to buy bonds of a eurozone member if yields rise uncontrollably and there is a risk of financial stress spreading.

However, most observers believe the problems in France do not yet meet the strict conditions stipulated for its use.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount
entries.summary: A ship in the Strait of Hormuz is reported to be on fire, a British maritime agency says. Iran has meanwhile said it has shot down another US drone as military tensions with Washington continue.
entries.content:
Iran

Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount

October 29, 2026

A ship in the Strait of Hormuz is reported to be on fire, a British maritime agency says. Iran has meanwhile said it has shot down another US drone as military tensions with Washington continue.

 A ship on fire has been reported in the Strait of Hormuz, British maritime agency UKMTO said on Thursday.

The agency, which is run by the British Royal Navy, did not give details on the cause of the blaze or any casualties.

Iran has, however, recently stepped up its attacks on ships that it sees as using the waterway without proper authorization.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route, but it is not known if the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them.

This comes as Iran has reported shooting down another US drone east of the waterway as fears grow of a new escalation in the US-Iran war. 

Iran steps up attacks in Strait of Hormuz

The UKMTO said the captain of another ship had reported the blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, which is located just off the strait.

The status of ⁠the ​crew is ​unknown, and so far ​no information has emerged pertaining to ⁠damage or environmental ⁠impact.

Since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers to be unauthorized users of the waterway.

Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler.

Attacks on ships in the strait are at the highest level since the war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.

US drone downed

The reported ship fire comes as Iran says its forces have downed a drone near the strait, with the Tasnim news agency citing the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used.

The report said that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out.

The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.

Fears of new US strikes

The latest incidents come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen to be considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Last week, Trump said, "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war. He did not, however, give any timeframe.

A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region.

As reports of a possible renewed escalation swirl, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly nonetheless fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia.

If confirmed, the ouster would be the latest in a series of such high-level departures under the Trump administration, with Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee being forced to retire last October.

According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches
entries.summary: Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis. 

"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.

"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.

"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.

"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."

Eberl, though, shut down the suggestion that this was related to pressure or stress.

"It's an illness. Any one of us can get it. It has nothing to do with the pressure we face in the Bundesliga," Eberl said.

Why do coaches push themselves so hard?

Nevertheless, with Kompany admitting he hadn't listened to his body and his assistant coach Aaron Danks saying that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge", it is clear that the Belgian had been working very hard of late.

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face in elite sport.

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that,"  coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."

Coaches in need of more support

It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?

"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.

"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.

"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.

"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.

"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."

Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.

"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.

"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."

Will change come to coaching?

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.

"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.

"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: India news: 'Cockroaches' back Gandhi's rally against election chief
entries.summary: The CJP said it would lend its support to any organization fighting for free and fair elections in India, including the opposition alliance. Also, India's right-wing RSS has a group of well wishers in the US. Follow DW.
entries.content:
India

India news: 'Cockroaches' back Gandhi's rally against election chief

Published October 29, 2026last updated October 29, 2026

The CJP said it would lend its support to any organization fighting for free and fair elections in India, including the opposition alliance. Also, India's right-wing RSS has a group of well wishers in the US. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India's Cockroach movement is throwing its weight behind Indian opposition's November 1 rally against the poll body chief
  • A group called 'RSS Friends' has registered itself in the US to step up outreach
  • Cyclone Arnab leaves devastation behind in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha

Here are the biggest headlines from India on Thursday, October 29: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Opposition bloc promises 'public impeachment' process against election chief

Opposition bloc promises 'public impeachment' process against election chief

Several leaders from India's opposition alliance, the INDIA bloc, have finalized the "public impeachment" proceedings they intend to carry out against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the controversial revision of voter lists. 

They did this in a meeting on Thursday at Indian National Congress (INC) President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence while he himself was in Bengaluru, local media reported.

They now plan to hold a mock Parliament sitting at Kharge's residence on Friday to conduct the "public impeachment" which is purely symbolic.

It will include speeches by opposition leaders, accounts by victims of the electoral roll revision, a motion passed by Kharge and a concluding speech by INC leader Rahul Gandhi. That's ahead of a planned November 1 rally to demand Kumar's removal.

The Election Commission of India began the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in 2025 to remove redundancies from India's electoral rolls including dead voters and those appearing more than once. Since then over 13 crore (130 Million) voter names have been deleted. There have also been reported irregularities allegedly on Kumar's part to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.

The BJP has denied allegations that the SIR exercise has benefited them, arguing it helped weed out "infiltrators" from the voter list.

On Tuesday, the INC claimed it was denied permission to hold the "public impeachment" of CEC Kumar at various venues, the Hindustan Times reported, and accused the government of trying to "silence" the voice of common people after "destroying" the electoral system.

Under law, the CEC can be removed by the Indian parliament through a process similar to the impeachment of a Supreme Court judge. He or she may also resign by submitting a written resignation to the president of India. 

Skip next section Odisha plans air evacuations from marooned villages

Odisha plans air evacuations from marooned villages

The east Indian state of Odisha is coordinating with the central Home Ministry to airlift people from the cyclone-struck Ganjam district where hundreds of villages remain inaccessible after heavy rain.

Ganjam was among some of the worst-affected districts in the state, authorities had earlier said. Some 300 villages there have been marooned due to heavy rain and flash floods, Press Trust of India reported citing a top state official.

Chief Secretary Anu Garg said teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and the Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force have begun rescue operations in the affected areas, but air evacuations could be delayed by low cloud level and continued rain.

Within Ganjam, Sorada village was among the worst affected with the Rushikulya river overflowing due to extremely heavy rainfall over the last three days.

Skip next section 'RSS Friends' registers in US to bolster outreach

'RSS Friends' registers in US to bolster outreach

A group of "well-wishers" of the India-based Rashtriya Sayamsevak Sangh (RSS) has registered with the US Department of Justice as a foreign agent of the right-wing Hindu nationalist group, news agency Press Trust of India reported on Thursday. 

The RSS is a 101-year-old organization with millions of followers across India. It presents itself as the guardian of Hindu values, while critics widely classify it as a paramilitary organization. Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has deep roots in the RSS, its influence reaches to the highest levels of political power. The Group is the ideological parent of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

'RSS Friends,' which provided a Georgia address for itself, listed a Delhi branch of RSS in India as its "foreign principal."

The group said its proposed activities are primarily informational, educational, public-relations and community-engagement activities.

"RSS Friends does not have a written employment, consulting, lobbying, public-relations, or agency agreement with RSS containing specified deliverables, compensation, or detailed operational instructions," the group said, adding that the lack of contract did not mean the connection did not exist.

The registration of RSS Friends was submitted two days before RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's outreach program at New York's Madison Square Garden on August 29. The controversial appearance is believed to be part of the RSS' global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. 

What else do we know about RSS Friends?

The group's website describes itself as a "dedicated well-wisher organization" seeking to address misrepresentation of RSS by US media or other "politically motivated actors."

Its social media, too, largely covered Bhagwat's NYC Event and has since been inactive.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Cyclone Arnab's trail of destruction:

IN PICTURES: Cyclone Arnab's trail of destruction:

Skip next section Cyclone Arnab damages homes and farmlands in eastern India

Cyclone Arnab damages homes and farmlands in eastern India

Cyclone Arnab on Wednesday battered Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, damaging homes, farmland and electricity infrastructure, authorities said. 

The cyclone made a prolonged landfall early Wednesday as a "very severe cyclonic storm" in the union territory of Puducherry and southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh. 

At least three people were killed even as the storm weakened while moving inland. Two women were electrocuted in separate incidents in the port city of Visakhapatnam, while another person was killed when a tree fell in East Godavari district, officials said.

Andhra Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu later said 14 of the state's districts were badly affected, requesting urgent assistance from the central government.

The cyclone damaged 79,000 acres of crops and dozens of homes. The worst hit area was the state's fertile Konaseema district where banana and coconut plantations suffered extensively.

While the eastern state of Odisha seemed to be less impacted initially, heavy rains and winds lashed several districts there on Wednesday evening. State authorities reported landslides, uprooted trees and damaged homes and infrastructure, but zero casualties.

On Thursday morning, Indian Home Minister Amit Shah reiterated the central government's support to the impacted states.

"In the wake of Cyclone Arnab, spoke with the Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha and Chhattisgarh and assured them of every assistance to mitigate the hardship of the people in the face of the disaster," he wrote in a post on X, adding that disaster relief teams were continuing operations on a "war footing."

Skip next section 'Cockroaches' back opposition-led rally against election chief

'Cockroaches' back opposition-led rally against election chief

Indian youth-led political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has decided to back the opposition bloc's upcoming November 1 rally, marking a shift in protest strategy.

The CJP said India's election commission has undermined people's right to choose their leaders through the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which allegedly deleted over 130 million names from voter lists across the country.

Election authorities said the list includes people who have died, moved away or were appearing on lists more than once, but critics argue the massive number is also likely to include a large number of eligible voters.

The CJP, several student organizations and opposition parties — with Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi at the helm — have been protesting against the revisions and alleged irregularities purported by India's election chief for over a month now. 

What else did the CJP say?

"Gyanesh Kumar has lost the trust required to oversee free and fair elections. His resignation is therefore necessary to restore the credibility and independence of the Election Commission," the CJP said in a statement published on X by founder Abhijeet Dipke.

"Our constitution gave every adult citizen the right to vote. It is our responsibility to ensure that no eligible citizen is deprived of that. The Cockroach Janta Party will therefore support all organizations fighting for free and fair election in our country," it said.

Dipke's caption read: "The Cockroach Janta Party extends its support to the INDIA Bloc's November 1 rally. Nation above all!"

The CJP and Gandhi's Indian National Congress have been running parallel campaigns so far with similar demands. However, they have not expressed direct support or held joint rallies before this, possibly in an effort not to alienate people who may relate to one group but not to the other.

However, the CJP now has limited choices. Its leaders were detained and arrested while protesting earlier this month and made to sign a peace bond which prohibits them from calling for mass protests in central Delhi. Lending their support to someone else's call for protest could be the loophole they needed.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! and welcome back to DW's India news blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi, where the weather is cooling down by the day but the Indian opposition's campaign against a controversial revision of electoral rolls is heating up.

After months of distance, India's Cockroach movement has thrown its weight behind the country's largest alliance of parties opposing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

This move came just days before an massive rally led by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, to demand poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and roll back the revision to voter lists.

What remains to be seen is if, when and how the Modi government will respond.

Speaking of chaos, a tropical cyclonic storm dubbed "Arnab" tore through India's east coast on Wednesday.

Local authorities in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, which faced the brunt of the storm, reported toppled trees, disrupted powers, and significant damage to property, crops and lives.

Moving away from home, India's largest right-wing "Hindutva" organization seems to have new "friends" in the US, looking to improve the group's image and gather support of Indians overseas.

entries.title: Spain train crash: PM Sanchez calls for investigation as 3 days of mourning begins
entries.summary: Emergency crews worked through the night after a high-speed train collision killed 68 people. PM Pedro Sanchez has pledged a full investigation into Spain's second major train accident this year.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain mourns train crash victims as rail safety questions loom

October 29, 2026

Emergency crews worked through the night after a high-speed train collision killed 68 people. PM Pedro Sanchez has pledged a full investigation into Spain's second major train accident this year.

Spain began three days of national mourning on Thursday in remembrance of the 68 people killed in one of Europe's deadliest train disasters in recent memory.

On Wednesday morning, a high-speed train run by state operator RENFE slammed into the back of a stationary train operated by private Italian-Spanish company Iryo in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid.

A British tourist who was rescued from the RENFE train told the Associated Press that "suddenly, everything started falling apart."

"We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over," the man said.

Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was on holiday in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the RENFE train when "I woke up and I was in the air."

Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, telling the AFP news agency that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.

He recounted "a very strong hit ... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos," while wearing a bloodstained jumper and holding a tattered suitcase. "I think I've been born again," he said.

Emergency crews work through the night

Emergency crews continued searching through the wreckage overnight for survivors and bodies, using cranes to move mangled metal.

Relatives of passengers gathered at nearby facilities seeking information about missing loved ones.

Residents of the nearby town of Urda joined emergency workers in helping survivors, providing first aid supplies, water and blankets.

Teams of Red Cross workers offered support.

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia told AFP news agency that many people are in shock and "haven't taken on board what has happened."

"The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.

Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to help identify the missing.

Spain's rail network safety in question

Wednesday's crash was Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year and has raised fresh questions about rail safety.

Transport Minister Oscar Puente blamed the crash on an "inexplicable" decision to allow one train to continue after an automatic control system failed along a stretch of track.

He said the RENFE high-speed train had travelled about 25 kilometers before hitting the stationary Iryo train.

Audio recordings reveal pre-crash exchanges

On Wednesday evening, Spanish media published audio recordings revealing confused conversations between the train drivers and the railways control center in the 30 minutes before the crash.

In one recording pubblished by the El Pais newspaper, among others, a control center operator appears to instruct the driver of the RENFE train to resume his journey at normal speed after some technical issues.

"Continue your journey and then proceed ... at normal speed [and] with normal operation," the operator tells the driver.

"At normal speed?" queries the driver, to which the controller confirms: "Yes."

A few minutes later, in another recording, the driver of the Iryo train then informs the control center that she is "stationary in front of the entry signal at [the town of] Urda" — about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) ahead of the RENFE train.

When she is still told to "resume the journey" normally, she says she cannot because of the security system error, reiterating that this is why she is stationary.

The second recording suggests therefore that the control center was aware of the stationary Iryo train having already instructed the RENFE train to travel towards it — but no further action appears to have been taken.

Spanish PM pledges full investigation

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who visited the crash site, pledged a full investigation and measures to strengthen rail safety.

"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sanchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."

In January, 46 people died when a high-speed train derailed and collided with another in the southern Andalusia region.

The latest disaster comes just weeks before Spain's November 29 general election which Prime Minister Sanchez had called hoping to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents — and distract from right-wing attacks on his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which they both deny.

About an hour before Wednesday's crash spread, Sanchez had posted a campaign message on social media reading: "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country."

Within 24 hours, Transport Minister Puente was facing calls to resign while Sanchez's main rival, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, demanded a full investigation of the crash and canceled campaign events for the day.

"This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Nunez Feijoo said. "But that does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers."

There was noticeably less restraint on show from Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, who will be hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives.

"More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," he said, refusing to join Nunez Feijoo's campaign pause.

"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead with nearly 90% of votes counted
entries.summary: With nearly 90% of votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc is just ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, but neither grouping is expected to win a majority, with tough coalition talks ahead. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc holds lead

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 29, 2026

With nearly 90% of votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc is just ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, but neither grouping is expected to win a majority, with tough coalition talks ahead. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
  • Latest vote count at 90% shows Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc holding the lead at 53 seats
  • Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot at 48 seats
  • At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
  • Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end

Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end

With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.

That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.

The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.

Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.

The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.

Skip next section Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots

Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.

Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.

According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.

This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.

The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.

Skip next section UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law. 

"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.

"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."

Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.

He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."

Skip next section 'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.

"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."

Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.

"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.

Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.

Skip next section WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.

Some small positives may be possible though.

Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.

Skip next section GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

Skip next section Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.

These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.

This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.

Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.

Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.

If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.

Skip next section President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.

"I will receive  the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions." 

Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.

"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments. 

Skip next section Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.

The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.

Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.

The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.

The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.

The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.

Skip next section Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu

Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu

The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.

"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.

"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."

After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.

As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.

Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."

However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.

Skip next section Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied

Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied

Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.

However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.

The results will change as counting progresses.

Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.

Skip next section Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties

Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties

Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.

"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.

"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.

Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.

Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.

Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.

Skip next section Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee

Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee

Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.

Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.

Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.

The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.

These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.

In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.

A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.

This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.

Skip next section Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election

Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.

"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.

"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.

Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.

Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.

Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

entries.title: North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles into sea
entries.summary: The latest ballistic missile launch comes amid rising border tensions with South Korea and uncertainty over potential nuclear talks with the US.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles into sea

October 29, 2026

The latest ballistic missile launch comes amid rising border tensions with South Korea and uncertainty over potential nuclear talks with the US.

North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said.

The missiles were launched at around 12:30 p.m. local time (0330 GMT) from an area near Wonsan on North Korea's eastern coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement.

South Korea's military said it was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness for additional launches while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.

Japan's Defense Ministry said the missiles had fallen outside the country's Exclusive Economic Zone, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency.

Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, most recently launching several short-range ballistic missiles on October 12.

Thursday's launch comes amid growing tensions between the two Koreas over a border dispute that has further strained relations between Seoul and Pyongyang.

Why are tensions rising between North and South Korea?

Three South Korean soldiers were wounded on September 21 when landmines exploded in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which separates the two countries.

A joint investigation by South Korea and the United Nations concluded earlier this month that North Korea had planted the landmines south of the military demarcation line more than a year ago.

Pyongyang has denied responsibility and warned of retaliation if provoked.

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned South Korean demands for an apology as "despicable." She also rejected Seoul's offer of medical equipment.

Last week, North Korea announced plans to resume propaganda broadcasts along the border and deploy new weapons systems in the area.

South Korea subsequently proposed talks to clarify the border and prevent accidental military clashes. Pyongyang has yet to respond.

What about potential US-North Korea nuclear talks?

The rising tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in potential nuclear negotiations.

Seoul is a key Washington ally, but Trump's approach has fueled uncertainty over South Korea's role in any future talks with the North.

North Korea's previous missile launch on October 12 came a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim Jong Un this year.

Edited by: Sean Sinico
